item.description:
It compresses the files it used to give up on

Ferry could only ever offer a file it had made itself — decode, re-encode, and if that came out bigger than what you dropped in, hand back your original and call it already good. It never asked the cheaper question: is this file carrying weight that isn't picture? Usually it is.

It now optimizes the file you gave it as well, losslessly, and weighs that against everything else. Screenshots that used to produce nothing now save 30–90%.

Two new formats, chosen per image

Ferry writes AVIF, WebP, JPEG and PNG, and picks by writing the candidates and measuring them rather than by guessing from the file type. WebP fills the gap that used to trap screenshots between a lossy codec that smeared the text and a PNG several megabytes wide: one 9 MB screenshot that came out at 6 MB now leaves at 106 kB.

JPEG picked up mozjpeg's optimizer, which rebuilds the coding tables for each image and writes progressively. About 9% smaller, with the decoded pixels identical.

Quality is measured, not set

A quality number can't know how hard a picture is to encode, so it overshoots badly on anything easy. Ferry now searches for the smallest encode that still clears its own fidelity bar, per image. On a document scan that meant 38% smaller with the text indistinguishable side by side.

Across a corpus of photographs: 88% average saving on Smallest, 78% on Works everywhere, and nothing refused on either.

Advanced, for when you know what you need

A third mode beside Smallest and Anywhere. Pin the format, or lossy against lossless, or both — useful when a pipeline or a client will only take one thing. Everything left on Auto is still decided by measuring; pinning narrows what Ferry may write, it doesn't switch the judgement off. When a pin forces something softer than Ferry would have picked, it says so.

Smaller things

Photographs shot on a phone are no longer misread as graphics, which used to leave a 24MP photo re-encoded at full size and beaten by its own original. The result screen leads with what happened rather than with a size increase when a conversion grew. Files that came out of a camera now say when their colors were converted to sRGB. The menu bar no longer spells out "Compressing" beside the boat. And an unlicensed copy no longer shows a blue verified badge next to the words "Not licensed".

Photos keep their own colour

Ferry used to fold an iPhone's HDR gain map back into the picture on the way out. On two thirds of photos that visibly changed the exposure — most often brighter, so faces washed out and lost detail — to reclaim a sliver of clipped highlight. Ferry now hands back the exposure the shot was metered for, the same rendition Photos exports.

The old behaviour is still there if you want it, and it now has a switch: Settings → HDR photos → Recover clipped highlights.

Photographs are checked before they're saved

Ferry has always measured its work on screenshots and logos, encoding a few versions and keeping the one that still looks right. Photographs skipped that check — they were saved at a fixed setting, sight unseen, and on more than half of them that setting was past the point Ferry would have accepted anywhere else. That's what made detail go soft and mushy.

Photographs now go through the same check as everything else. If the first attempt gives up too much, Ferry spends the bytes and tries again. Most photos are unaffected; the ones that were being quietly ruined come out visibly better, and a little larger.

You can keep every pixel

The resize setting only ever made images smaller, so on a photograph — already brought down to 2000px for the web — every size it offered did nothing at all. It now sets the size, in both directions, and there's an Original size option for keeping the full resolution.

Left alone, Ferry still brings photographs down to 2000px. That's where most of the saving comes from. If you had already picked a size in Settings, it now does what it says — which may mean larger files than you were getting.

Smaller files

Every AVIF Ferry wrote claimed to have transparency, even a photograph that plainly doesn't, and paid about 1% of its size to say so. Fixed.
